name: Strategic Planning and Scenarios
title: Strategic Planning and Scenarios
answer: A strategic plan for AI gives a district a clear direction by naming goals tied to student learning and staff time, the rules that govern AI use, the pilots underway, and how results will be measured. Scenario planning and AI related crisis communication plans prepare leaders for vendor failures, new restrictions, data breaches and harmful incidents. The goals and priorities must come from district leaders and the community, because a plan written mostly by a tool will not guide real decisions.

sections.body: This idea is a planning discipline for districts that are adopting AI. A strategic plan sets direction by naming goals tied to student learning and staff time, the rules that govern AI use, the pilots underway, and how results will be measured. Scenario planning then asks what happens if a major vendor fails, if new laws restrict certain uses of AI, or if a data breach exposes student information. Crisis communication planning extends the same thinking to AI related incidents such as a deepfake of a staff member, a chatbot giving harmful advice to a student, or a breach at an AI vendor. The problem it solves is uncertainty, because talking through scenarios in advance makes a district more resilient and prepared templates make fast, honest communication possible when something goes wrong.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a district, the work starts with leaders and the community setting the goals and priorities, while AI may help draft sections of the plan. The plan itself should name the goals tied to student learning and staff time, the rules governing AI use, the pilots underway, and the measures for results. Leaders then talk through scenarios in advance, including a major vendor failing, new laws restricting certain uses of AI, and a data breach exposing student information. Crisis communication planning adds AI related scenarios, such as a deepfake of a staff member, a chatbot giving harmful advice to a student, or a breach at an AI vendor, with templates prepared and reviewed ahead of time. The supplied text does not give grade band variations for this idea, so it is described here at the district and school leadership level.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no research label and no study for strategic planning and scenario planning as practices. Its one concrete reference is the Los Angeles case of a major vendor failing, cited as EdSurge, 2024. Beyond that, the idea rests on practice and on the judgement of district leaders rather than on research evidence. The text also says the principles from Chapter 14 apply to crisis communication, without stating any findings from them.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text is clear that the goals and priorities must come from the district's leaders and community, not from a tool. AI can help draft sections of the plan, but a plan written mostly by a tool will not guide real decisions. That keeps the substantive choices, about what the district is trying to achieve and how it will measure results, with people. Crisis communication also carries a human obligation, since a deepfake of a staff member, a chatbot giving harmful advice to a student, or a breach at an AI vendor each require fast, honest communication, which is why templates should be reviewed in advance.
